text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Aug 12 editions of Russia's newspapers. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- The latest outburst of fighting in Tajikistan came as a surprise both for Dushanbe and Moscow.

- Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko's public announcement he was ready to host a meeting between Russian President Yeltsin and separatist Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov put Moscow, which considers Chechnya as part of Russia, in an awkward situation.
- Russian truck producer KamAZ has annuled its agreements with two U.S. investment companies.
- Five thousand Russian managers will go abroad for training under a new government scheme.
- Foreign enterpreneurs should not beware of running a business in Russia, provided they stick to certain rules and do not economise on security.
- Russia could suffer huge grain losses while bringing in the 1997 harvest if it fails to take urgent measures to save the crop.
- The state budget will receive a big boost once the money lingering in the accounts of the Customs Committee at commercial banks are transferred to the Central Bank.
- A persistent energy crisis in Russia's Far East, barely put down in June, is threatening to flare up again.

- Uneximbank's daughter company Renaissance Capital International Ltd. has good chances of winning a contest to advise the energy monopoly Unified Energy Systems of Russia on an issue of convertible bonds.
- There is no doubt that despite all posible negative moments a rapprochement between Moscow and Minsk meets Russia's interests.
- A large-scale army reform, kick-started by fresh-faced reformers in the government, seems to be ignoring the interests of many ordinary servicemen and their families.
- A high-profile scandal involving certain commercial banks and former top government officials may be far from over in the face of new evidence of alleged theft from state coffers.
- A years-long fight between reformers and conservatives in Russian leadership seems to have turned into nothing more but a confusing struggle since the last government shake-up.
